title: The Prime 2 Breaks the Odd-Prime Pattern
content: For an odd prime p, every 1 + p·a (p ∤ a) attains the maximal p-power order p^(k-1), and (ℤ/pᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic. At p = 2 both statements fail. The maximal 2-power order 2^(k-2) is carried only by the principal units 1 + 4ℤ (generated by 5), not by all of 1 + 2ℤ; and the unit group is non-cyclic for k ≥ 3 because it has two distinct involutions. This file makes both phenomena precise and gives a constructive non-cyclicity proof.

title: The Corresponding Order Needs 1 + 4·a
content: The p = 2 analogue of the parent's orderOf(1 + p·a) = p^(k-1) is orderOf(1 + 4·a) = 2^(k-2) for odd a — note 4·a, not 2·a. Re-exported from Mathlib's ZMod.orderOf_one_add_four_mul. The factor 4 (rather than 2) is forced: an element 1 + 2·a with a odd lies in the ≡ 3 mod 4 coset and does not generate the maximal cyclic 2-group.
mathContext: $\mathrm{ord}_{(\mathbb{Z}/2^{n+2})^\times}(1 + 4a) = 2^n$ for odd $a$; $5 = 1 + 4$ is the textbook generator.

title: The Special Involution 1 + 2^(k-1)
content: Modulo 2^k the element 1 + 2^(k-1) squares to 1, because (1 + 2^(k-1))² = 1 + 2^k + 2^(2k-2) and both extra terms are divisible by 2^k. Combined with 1 + 2^(k-1) ≠ 1, the prime-order criterion orderOf_eq_prime gives it order exactly 2. The squaring identity is proved through a natural-number congruence (1 + 2^(n+2))² ≡ 1 [MOD 2^(n+3)], keeping the argument axiom-free.

title: Non-Cyclicity from Two Involutions
content: A finite cyclic group has exactly φ(2) = 1 element of order 2. The unit group (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ has two: −1 (order 2 since ringChar = 2^k ≠ 2) and 1 + 2^(k-1) (the special involution). They are distinct for k ≥ 3. Counting order-2 elements with IsCyclic.card_orderOf_eq_totient then forces a contradiction, proving (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ is not cyclic. This names the obstruction explicitly, unlike the reduction-based proof in Mathlib.

title: Cyclicity Dichotomy and Concrete Instances
content: Re-exporting ZMod.isCyclic_units_two_pow_iff records that (ℤ/2ᵏℤ)ˣ is cyclic iff k ≤ 2, isolating 2^k (k ≥ 3) as the unique non-cyclic prime power once the odd-prime case is known cyclic. The concrete corollaries (¬ IsCyclic (ℤ/8ℤ)ˣ, orderOf(−1 : ℤ/8ℤ) = 2, orderOf(5 : ℤ/8ℤ) = 2) are all instances of the general theorems, obtained without native_decide.
mathContext: $(\mathbb{Z}/2^k\mathbb{Z})^\times$ cyclic $\iff k \le 2$; smallest non-cyclic case $k = 3$ is $(\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z})^\times \cong \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2$.
